beats.headline: Java has zero concept of truthy or falsy values.
beats.subline: Writing if (1) or if (username) will instantly halt your compilation.
beats.narration: Java has zero concept of truthy or falsy values. Writing if open parenthesis one close parenthesis in Java stops javac dead in its tracks. Let's see how strict boolean checks protect your codebase.

beats.title: Scripting Truthy vs. Strict Java Booleans

top.label: C / JavaScript
top.code:
if (1) { /* runs */ }
if (username) { /* runs if non-empty */ }
points: Numbers and pointers convert to boolean
Permissive syntax leads to subtle type bugs

bottom.label: Standard Java
points: Condition must evaluate strictly to true or false
Prevents unintentional type coercions at compile time

beats.narration: Languages like Python or JavaScript convert numbers and objects to booleans. Java rejects this outright. Every condition in an if statement or loop must evaluate strictly to a true or false boolean.

beats.title: Short-Circuit Evaluation Guard

steps.explanation: Evaluates left to right. If user is null, left is false, so user.isActive() is never called.
Evaluates both operands regardless of left result, throwing NullPointerException when user is null.

beats.narration: Double ampersand short-circuits. If user is null, the right side is never called. But single ampersand evaluates both sides unconditionally, triggering a NullPointerException when user is null.

beats.title: Silent Boolean Assignment Trap

steps.explanation: Assigns true to isVerified and returns boolean true, causing the block to run unconditionally!
Clean and safe boolean condition with zero assignment risk.

beats.narration: Single equals inside an if check assigns true to the boolean variable and evaluates to true. The block executes unconditionally. Test the boolean directly to prevent this security bug.

beats.title: Part 1 Control Flow Secured
takeaways: Avoid boolean assignment traps inside if headers

beats.headline: A missing break statement can bypass security.
beats.subline: Classic C-style switch fall-through is one of software history's oldest bug sources.
beats.narration: Forgetting a single break statement in a classic switch can silently execute unauthorized branches. Modern Java fixed this design flaw.

beats.title: Classic Switch vs. Modern Switch Expression

top.label: Classic Switch (Java 1+)

bottom.label: Arrow Switch Expression (Java 14+)

beats.narration: Classic switch statements fall through into subsequent cases unless you write break. Java 14 introduced arrow switch expressions, eliminating fall-through, supporting comma-separated constants, and returning values directly.

beats.title: Multi-Statement Branches with yield

steps.explanation: Hands a final result back to the switch expression from inside multi-statement block braces.
Required for open type sets like int or String to guarantee compile-time exhaustiveness.

beats.narration: When an arrow branch needs multiple statements, wrap the branch in curly braces and return the final value using yield. Never use return here, because return exits the entire method.

beats.title: Java 21 Pattern Matching for switch

steps.explanation: Direct null handling eliminates NullPointerException inside switch evaluations.
Guards check secondary boolean expressions before matching open object bindings.

beats.narration: Java 21 finalized pattern matching for switch. You can match object types directly, evaluate null safely without extra guards, and add boolean when clauses to filter branch conditions.

beats.title: Switch Mastery Unlocked
takeaways: Use yield for multi-line block results
Pattern matching handles null and type guards

beats.narration: Modern switch expressions keep code safe and concise. Up next in Part 3: loop selection rules and the silent collection modification crash.

beats.headline: Mutating collections in for-each crashes production.
beats.subline: Calling list.remove() inside an enhanced loop triggers immediate runtime failure.
beats.narration: Calling list dot remove inside an enhanced for-each loop throws a ConcurrentModificationException at runtime. Here is why it fails and how to fix it.

beats.title: Java Loop Lifecycle Comparison
beats.subtitle: Choosing the right loop construct for your execution needs

nodes.label: Classic for Loop
nodes.detail: Explicit index counter, condition checked before body, ideal for array bounds

nodes.label: while Loop
nodes.detail: Condition checked before body, runs 0 or more times based on external state

nodes.label: do-while Loop
nodes.detail: Body runs first, condition checked after, guaranteed to run at least once

nodes.label: Enhanced for-each
nodes.detail: Desugars into Iterator operations, safe traversal over collections

beats.narration: Classic for loops give explicit index control. While loops check conditions before execution. Do-while loops guarantee at least one iteration cycle, and enhanced for-each loops simplify safe collection reading.

beats.title: Modifying Collections in For-Each
beats.caption: Internal modification counter mismatch failure
beats.narration: Under the hood, for-each creates an Iterator. Modifying the collection directly changes its modification counter, causing the iterator to detect a mismatch on the next iteration and crash.

beats.title: Safe Collection Removal

steps.explanation: Bypasses the underlying Iterator state, corrupting expected modification count.
Safely removes matching elements in bulk without invalidating iterator state.

beats.narration: Never mutate a collection directly inside a for-each loop. Use removeIf on the list, or manage an explicit Iterator and call iterator dot remove to update safely.

beats.title: Loop Mechanics Mastered
takeaways: For-each converts to Iterator under the hood
Use removeIf for clean element filtering

beats.narration: That covers loop mechanics and mutation safety. Up next in Part 4: labeled breaks, continue traps, and escaping nested loops cleanly.

beats.headline: Standard break only exits your innermost loop.
beats.subline: Nested matrix processing will keep executing outer loops silently.
beats.narration: Calling break inside a nested loop only exits the inner loop, leaving your outer loop running silently. Let's fix this logic trap.

beats.title: The While Loop Continue Trap

steps.explanation: Jumps straight back to while condition check, skipping the counter increment on line 8!

beats.narration: In a for loop, continue executes the counter update. In a while loop, continue jumps straight back to the condition check. If the increment sits below continue, your loop runs forever.

beats.title: Labeled Break for Multi-Dimensional Matrix

steps.explanation: Labels the outer loop block so jump targets can specify enclosing scope.
Terminates both inner and outer loops simultaneously without boolean flag boilerplate.

beats.narration: Unqualified break only exits the innermost loop. Attaching a label like search to your outer loop allows break search to terminate both nested loops instantly without complex boolean flags.

beats.title: Loop Control Keywords Compared

top.label: break vs. continue
top.code:
break;    // Exits innermost loop body
continue; // Skips to next iteration cycle
points: Labeled versions target specific outer loops

bottom.label: return
bottom.code: return result; // Exits entire enclosing method
points: Passes result back to caller context

beats.narration: Break exits the current loop block completely. Continue skips the rest of the current cycle and advances to the next. Return exits the entire enclosing method, terminating all active loops.

beats.title: Loop Disruption Locked In
takeaways: Continue in while loops can cause infinite loops
Labeled breaks escape nested outer loops cleanly
Return terminates all active loops by exiting method

parts.partTitle: Hardware Branch Prediction & Control Flow Mastery

beats.headline: Unsorted data in loops can slow your CPU by 5x.
beats.subline: CPU hardware branch predictors mispredict random branching conditions constantly.
beats.narration: Evaluating an if condition over unsorted data can slow down your CPU execution by 5x due to hardware branch mispredictions.

beats.title: Hardware Branch Predictor Pipeline
beats.subtitle: How modern CPUs execute conditional instructions speculatively

nodes.label: Instruction Pipeline
nodes.detail: Overlaps CPU instruction execution steps for high throughput

nodes.label: Branch Predictor
nodes.detail: Guesses if/else branch direction before evaluation completes

nodes.label: Correct Guess
nodes.detail: Execution pipeline flows seamlessly at full CPU speed

nodes.label: Misprediction Flush
nodes.detail: Pipeline flushes speculative instructions, losing 15+ cycles

beats.narration: Modern CPUs do not wait for branch conditions to finish. They predict which path your code will take. Correct predictions execute smoothly, while mispredictions flush the pipeline and waste clock cycles.

beats.title: Branch Prediction Microbenchmark
beats.caption: Sorted vs. unsorted array processing time comparison

lines.text: JIT Compiler optimizes hot loops automatically

beats.narration: Processing sorted data lets the CPU branch predictor guess accurately almost every time. Processing random unsorted data triggers constant pipeline flushes, executing over five times slower.

beats.title: Modern Clean Control Flow

steps.explanation: Early exit handling prevents deep nesting and guards null inputs safely.
Clean arrow syntax returns values directly with compiler-checked exhaustiveness.

beats.narration: Modern Java combines strict guard clauses with exhaustive arrow switch expressions. You get complete type safety, zero fall-through bugs, and clean readable code that JIT compilers optimize seamlessly.

beats.title: Control Flow Chapter Complete
takeaways: Short-circuit booleans guard against null errors
Arrow switch expressions replace fall-through bugs
Hardware branch prediction rewards predictable control flow
